g.text: db.applyMu.RLock — one hold spans traversal and metadata

div.h3: Readers never wait on a writer's I/O
div.p: applyMu is held exclusively only for the apply itself — never across the WAL append or fsync, which sit under writeMu, a lock no reader takes. So the most a search waits for is one apply; large batches apply in groups of applyGroup and release between them.
Snapshots hold writeMu, not these locks — searches keep running through one.

div.h3: Why the graph search is 1 alloc/op

ul.li: visited set — generation-stamped []uint32, not a map[int]struct{}. Clearing is gen++, O(1), no alloc.
heaps — plain []candidate with hand-written sift up/down. container/heap passes values as any, which boxes every candidate.
searchLayer's output lives in the state too (st.found).
The one allocation is the []Result handed back (BenchmarkSearch, and BenchmarkSearchFilter filtered). The DB adds the []Match and the metadata copies.

div.p: This scratch is per-traversal, not graph-owned. It comes from a pooled searchState, which is what lets Search hold only RLock and run in parallel — graph-owned buffers would make concurrent searches corrupt each other.

Bigger = wider layer-0 search = higher recall, slower. Recall at a fixed ef falls as N or dimension grows, so leave Ef at 0 and set TargetRecall instead. Calibrate (leave-one-out, background, re-run when the live count doubles or halves) corrects the formula for how hard this data is.
Locked baselines: recall@10 = 0.999 at dim 32, 0.988 at dim 768, against brute force in graph_test.go.
M is structural — changing it requires a rebuild.

closed atomic → ErrClosed query: right dimension, every value finite (one NaN poisons the ordering) 1 ≤ K ≤ maxK · 0 ≤ Ef ≤ maxEf · 0 ≤ TargetRecall < 1 Filter.Validate() once, here — never per node → ErrInvalidFilter

Ef == 0 means "choose it": SuggestedEf(K, target) — target defaults to 0.95 fitted ef ∝ n^0.78 · k^0.2 · (16/M)^0.85 × efScale from the last Calibrate (1 until one runs) clamped to maxEf, then max(ef, K)
allow(id) = store.Match(id, f.Match) over ids, not metadata — the index never sees a second data model. Match does not copy: 0 allocs, it runs once per candidate node

g.text: g.mu.RLock — RAM only, parallel with other searches

div.p: Returns fewer than k. Measured at one-in-fifty selectivity: 10 results in-traversal, 2 post-filtered. Same mistake as filtering tombstones at the end — which is why admits() holds both checks.
div.h3: "Get indices from HNSW, then fetch vectors from disk"
div.p: The graph needs a vector at every hop to compute the next distance — hundreds of lookups per query. Backing vectors with disk is not a slower HNSW, it is a different and much worse algorithm. Disk-friendly traversal is DiskANN — a different index, out of scope.
searchState from a sync.Pool Cosine: copy into st.queryBuf and normalize — the caller's slice is never touched, and this runs before the graph lock: the buffer is ours
searchLayer returns ascending, so w[:k] → []Result{ID, Distance} — the graph's one allocation — then the adapter retypes to []Match
store.Get(id) per match — an in-RAM store.Map, returned as a copy so a caller cannot mutate the store. Under the same applyMu hold as the traversal, so no result pairs v2 with md1.
Step to the closest neighbor until none improves. Unfiltered and tombstone-blind: pure routing, the node it lands on is a seed, never an answer.
Best-first on layer 0, the only layer holding every vector.

Gather · touch · score per expansion: unvisited neighbors into st.fresh, one float per 128 B line each (touchLines) so all misses are in flight, then distances in the original order — 1.7–1.9×, bit-identical.
cands (min-heap frontier) admits everything — a tombstone or a filtered-out node is still a bridge. results (max-heap, worst at top) admits only admits(): live and allow(id).
Stop when the nearest frontier node is farther than the worst of ef results.
